title: Platformers
blurb: Crash and Spyro anchor a chapter of mascot platformers that helped define the PS1's identity, alongside a scrappy British entry that beat its own Japanese release to market.
games: The spin-attacking marsupial that became Sony's first mascot, built by Naughty Dog around aggressively tight level design and a signature save-crystal structure.
A sequel that added the jet pack and a wider toolkit of moves, widely seen as tightening everything the original got right.
The trilogy's high point, breaking up its platforming with motorbike, jet-ski, and biplane stages for real variety between levels.
A fully explorable, seamless 3D hub-world structure was rare for its time, wrapped around Spyro's charm, gliding, and gem-collecting loop.

Released across Europe as Spyro 2: Gateway to Glimmer rather than Ripto's Rage — one of this collection's clearest title swaps — while adding swimming and new powered abilities to the original's formula.
The trilogy's closer, adding four extra playable characters alongside Spyro and pushing the series' draw distance and world size further than before.
A hand-animated, limbless hero from French studio Ubi Soft, built around some of the most punishing platforming difficulty of the era.

Released in the West months before its own Japanese release (where it carried the different title Croc! Pau Pau Island) — an unusually reversed rollout for the era — this British-developed mascot platformer was originally conceived as a Yoshi game before becoming its own IP.
A 2.5D platformer blending flat side-scrolling movement with a fully 3D dreamlike world, built around a signature double-jump-off-enemies mechanic.

title: Action-Adventure
blurb: Lara Croft and Solid Snake anchor a chapter of genre-defining 3D action-adventure, including two titles built by British studios that became global landmarks in their own right.
games: A British-developed 3D adventure that made Lara Croft one of gaming's first true global icons, built around tank-control platforming and tomb-puzzle exploration.
A more combat-focused, faster-paced sequel adding vehicles and a wider arsenal to the original's exploration formula.
Lets players tackle its globe-spanning levels in almost any order, trading the earlier games' linear structure for open-ended choice.
Hideo Kojima's cinematic reinvention of stealth action, built around avoiding detection rather than confrontation and a script unusually invested in film-style pacing.
A puzzle-platformer with a genuinely strange tone, built around Abe's ability to possess enemies and a GameSpeak system for directing fellow slaves.
A direct sequel expanding the original's mechanics with new powers and a much larger, more varied set of environments.
A British-made gothic-horror-comedy platformer starring a resurrected, famously incompetent knight, with a tone unlike almost anything else on the console.
A top-down action-adventure often compared to Zelda, built around genuinely difficult, physics-based puzzle design that outpaced its own commercial success.

title: Survival Horror
blurb: Resident Evil effectively invented the genre's console template here, in a chapter that also holds its most atmospheric psychological successor.
games: Defined the survival-horror template almost single-handedly, pairing fixed camera angles and tank controls with deliberately scarce ammunition.
Widely regarded as the series' peak on PS1, running two interlocking scenarios (Leon and Claire) through the same zombie-overrun police station.
Introduces the Nemesis, a pursuing enemy that can appear almost anywhere in the game rather than staying confined to scripted encounters.
Traded Resident Evil's B-movie zombies for genuine psychological dread, with the town's famous fog originally a technical workaround that became a defining artistic choice.
Essentially 'Resident Evil with dinosaurs,' built by much of the same team and swapping the undead for genuinely unpredictable predators.
A point-and-click survival horror game built around evasion rather than combat, chased throughout by the unkillable Scissorman.
An unusual hybrid of turn-based RPG combat and survival horror, based on a Japanese novel about spontaneous human combustion and mitochondrial rebellion.

title: Role-Playing Adventures
blurb: The genre PS1 is remembered for above all else — Square and Konami's golden age, including several celebrated RPGs that, unusually, never made it to Europe at all.
games: The game most responsible for bringing console RPGs into the mainstream West, built around pre-rendered backgrounds and then-unprecedented CGI cutscenes.
Trades the series' traditional leveling system for the Junction mechanic, tying stat growth directly to a much deeper magic system.
A deliberate return to the series' classic fantasy aesthetic after two increasingly futuristic entries, built as a love letter to its own earlier games.
A tactical-RPG spin-off with a surprisingly dense political plot, built on an isometric grid battle system that spawned its own sub-genre of imitators.
An ambitious blend of philosophical, Gnostic-influenced storytelling with giant-mech combat — one of the few major Squaresoft RPGs of the era that never received any European PS1 release at all.
A spiritual successor to Chrono Trigger with a completely different cast and setting, notable for a soundtrack widely considered one of the format's best.
A dense, mechanically deep action-RPG set entirely within one abandoned city, built around a weapon-crafting and armor-break system rarely attempted since.
Built around recruiting all 108 of the 'Stars of Destiny' into a growing castle headquarters, a collection hook the series became known for.
A direct sequel widely regarded as one of the best RPGs of its generation — and, thanks to a small print run, now one of the most expensive PS1 discs to collect.
A four-disc epic built around the Dragoon transformations its title characters can call on mid-battle, timed-hit combat layered on top of traditional turn-based structure.
Follows a dragon-blooded protagonist who ages in real time across the story, with combat built around his ability to transform into different dragon forms.
An early example of blending real-time movement with turn-based combat on the same battlefield, letting positioning interrupt enemy attacks directly.

title: Fighting
blurb: Tekken's rise to the genre's top tier happened here, alongside a one-hit-kill sword duelist that rejected nearly every convention of the genre around it.
games: A launch-era 3D fighter built on genuinely fluid character movement, establishing the series' signature four-limb-independent control scheme.
Expands the roster substantially and refines the original's combo system, widely seen as tightening everything the first game established.
Often cited as the high point of the PS1 fighting genre, adding sidestepping and a noticeably faster, more fluid combat rhythm.
Brings the arcade original's huge character roster and three selectable fighting styles (Ism system) to console with minimal compromise.
Rejects health bars entirely in favor of realistic sword combat where a single well-placed hit can end the match outright.

Released in the West as Soul Blade rather than its Japanese title, Soul Edge, reportedly to avoid a trademark conflict — the European version also swapped one character's nunchaku for a censor-friendly staff.
Sets its fighting-game roster inside rival Japanese high schools, with two-character tag teams and story-driven presentation unusual for the genre.
Lets fighters transform mid-match into beast forms with entirely different movesets, a gimmick that gave the series its own identity in a crowded genre.

title: Racing
blurb: Gran Turismo's arrival redefined what a racing sim could be on console, in a chapter also carrying two moody, electronic-music-scored British flagship titles.
games: Marketed as 'the real driving simulator,' its enormous, meticulously modeled car roster reset expectations for what a console racer could be.
Roughly doubles the original's car count and adds rally courses, becoming one of the best-selling PS1 games in the process.
An arcade racer built entirely around drift technique, wrapped in one of the console era's most distinctive anime-style intro sequences.
A British-developed anti-gravity racer whose licensed electronic soundtrack (Chemical Brothers, Orbital) helped define PS1's early cool-factor image in Europe.

Released in North America as Wipeout XL rather than keeping the European title — one of the platform's clearer NA-side renames, running the opposite direction from most of this collection's title swaps.
A mascot kart racer built to compete directly with Mario Kart, adding a full adventure mode with boss battles on top of standard cup racing.
A British-developed rally sim built around genuine surface-grip physics, launching a long-running franchise named for the real-world Scottish rally driver.
An early PS1 title built almost entirely around vehicle-damage physics, turning car-crushing itself into the actual objective rather than a side effect.

title: Sports
blurb: A chapter of arcade-leaning sports titles anchored by the direct ancestor of the Pro Evolution Soccer series, sold under two different names on either side of the Atlantic.
games: Released across Europe under the fuller International Superstar Soccer Pro Evolution branding roughly a year before reaching North America at all under the shortened ISS name — the direct predecessor to the entire Pro Evolution Soccer series.
A British-developed early entry in 3D football sims, built to compete directly with FIFA's arcade-leaning presentation.
Timed to that year's World Cup, adding every qualifying national team alongside the usual club rosters.
An arcade-accessible golf game built around a simple three-click swing meter, launching a long-running series sold in Europe as Everybody's Golf.
Turned skateboarding into a combo-scoring arcade genre almost overnight, its soundtrack becoming as iconic as the gameplay itself.
Leans fully into arcade excess — no fouls, exaggerated dunks, and an 'on fire' streak mechanic — over basketball simulation.
A button-mashing multi-event Olympic compilation, known in Japan under the Hyper Olympic name its earlier arcade entries used.

title: Puzzle & Party
blurb: Point Blank's light-gun mini-games anchor a chapter that also holds one of the PS1's strangest rhythm curios — a game that took fifteen years to reach North America.
games: Adds a dedicated Puzzle mode with block-clearing objectives on top of the standard endless mode, aimed at Tetris veterans wanting a new challenge structure.
A bubble-shooting puzzle sequel best known for its two-player versus mode, built on the same core aim-and-match mechanic as the arcade original.
A light-gun mini-game collection with an enormous arcade pedigree, built around dozens of short, escalating shooting-gallery challenges.

Released across Europe as Kurushi, actually reaching PAL shelves ahead of its own North American release — a minimalist puzzle game about stopping advancing cube formations before they crush the player.
A dice-matching puzzle-strategy hybrid that would later return, retooled, as the PS2's Bombastic — one of the more unusual puzzle concepts on the platform.

A minimalist wireframe rhythm game that generates its courses from whatever music CD is in the player's own console — and, unusually, never received a North American PS1 release at all, only reaching the region 15 years later via PS3.

title: Simulation & Strategy
blurb: British studios anchor this chapter almost entirely — Bullfrog and Team17's genre-founding console ports sit alongside a serious-toned tactical RPG.
games: A British-made reinvention of the god-game genre Bullfrog itself founded, moving from 2D terrain manipulation to a fully 3D world.
A console port of the PC real-time strategy hit, built around an alternate-history setting where Einstein erases Hitler from time entirely.
A turn-based artillery-strategy classic from another British studio, built around an enormous, joke-filled arsenal of increasingly absurd weapons.
A fully 3D take on the farming-sim formula, deepening the original series' day-and-season cycle with more detailed town and relationship systems.
A British hospital-management sim laced with dry humor, tasking players with treating patients suffering from deliberately absurd fictional illnesses.
The first Front Mission to reach the West at all, built around deep mecha customization and a story that branches based on an early player choice.
A tactical RPG with a noticeably grimmer, war-drama tone than most of its genre peers, built on a hex-grid battle system.

title: Licensed & Movie Tie-ins
blurb: Die Hard Trilogy's three genres on one disc anchors a chapter of largely well-regarded licensed titles from an era before movie tie-ins had a reputation for being rushed.
games: A first-person shooter built entirely around the animated show's crude humor, using clay-animation-style character models to match the show's look.
A British-developed anthology squeezing three separate genres — rail shooter, third-person action, and driving — onto one disc, each tied to a different film in the series.
A British-developed licensed platformer tracking the film's story beats, mixing on-foot combat with several distinct minigame styles.
A licensed action game built around the film's toy-soldiers-come-to-life premise, letting players command a squad through household-scale battlefields.
A trivia-and-minigame party title built around the film's catchphrases and characters rather than a traditional action adaptation.
A well-regarded web-slinging action game built with a genuine sense of verticality, later credited as one of the better licensed superhero games of its era.

title: Cult Classics & Deep Cuts
blurb: PaRappa the Rapper invented an entire genre here, in a chapter carrying the deepest run of confirmed Europe-skipping Square RPGs found in this project yet.
games: One of the earliest true 3D platformers on any console, played from a first-person perspective as a robotic rabbit bouncing through vertically-stacked levels.
An unusually dark, mechanically demanding side-scrolling shooter from a studio mostly known for RPGs — one of several Square titles from this era that never received any European PS1 release.
Effectively invented the modern rhythm-action genre, built around a flat, paper-cutout art style and call-and-response rap battles.
A stylistic sequel to PaRappa swapping rapping for guitar riffs, starring a guitarist whose skill is inversely tied to how panicked she becomes.
An anthropomorphic-animal action-adventure that, unusually, reached a France-exclusive European release nearly a year before its own North American debut.
A hybrid of randomized dungeon-crawling and town-building, letting players raise monster allies that carry over between runs.
An action-RPG starring a sword-wielding hero summoned to save a kingdom on a strict in-game deadline — another Square RPG of this era that never made it to Europe on PS1.

Released in Japan as Dewprism, this action-RPG lets players replay its entire story from either of two different protagonists' perspectives — and, like several Square RPGs of the era, never received a European PS1 release.
A turn-based RPG whose combat runs on a unique directional-input combo system, closer to a fighting game's move list than typical menu-driven battles.

title: Arcade Ports & Multiplayer Curios
blurb: The largest chapter in the collection, gathering vehicular-combat launch titles, British sci-fi flight sims, and party-focused multiplayer curios built around the console's four-player adapter.
games: A launch-era vehicular combat game pitting armed cars against each other in a demolition-derby-meets-deathmatch format.
A sequel expanding the roster and arenas considerably, widely considered the series' high point on PS1.
The first game built specifically around the DualShock's analog sticks, tasking players with net-capturing escaped monkeys across time-travel-themed levels.
Brings the series' classic grid-based, four-player bomb-battle format to PS1 largely unchanged from its earlier console outings.
A kart-racing spin-off starring the Bomberman cast, trading grid-based battles for lap-based races with bomb-throwing power-ups.
A British-developed miniature-vehicle racer fitting up to eight players onto household-scale tracks — kitchen counters, garden hoses, and pool tables among them.
A port of the giant-monster arcade brawler, letting up to three players smash city skylines as an oversized ape, lizard, or werewolf.
A British-developed atmospheric flight-combat game set in a rain-soaked, cyberpunk-styled off-world colony, built around genuinely moody sci-fi world-building.
A cinematic space-combat sim from the same British studio behind G-Police, built around branching missions that respond to whether the player wins or loses.
A futuristic hover-bike racer built around aggressive, physics-heavy track design full of shortcuts and vertical drops.
A Mario Party-style multiplayer spin-off built entirely around the Crash Bandicoot cast, trading platforming for competitive minigames.
Launched what would become a long-running wrestling series, moving beyond the earlier WWF console games toward a fuller, more simulation-leaning in-ring engine.
Swaps the mainline series' first-person perspective for third-person, time-travel-themed levels — a deliberate departure from the main FPS games.
